nameStory: Common valerian gets its name from the Latin 'valere,' meaning 'to be strong' or 'to be well,' referring to its powerful medicinal properties that have been valued for over 2,000 years. The 'officinalis' part of its scientific name means 'of the workshop' - indicating this was an official plant sold in medieval apothecaries. Ancient Greeks and Romans used it as a remedy for insomnia and anxiety, and it's still sold as an herbal sleep aid today.
description: Common valerian is a tall, clump-forming perennial herb that can reach 3-5 feet in height. It produces clusters of small, sweetly fragrant pink or white flowers at the top of sturdy stems in summer. The plant has deeply divided, feathery leaves that grow in pairs along the stem. While the flowers smell pleasant, the roots have a distinctly strong, musky odor that cats find irresistible - it's actually more potent than catnip for our feline friends!

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Dense, rounded clusters of tiny tubular flowers, each about 1/8 inch across, ranging from pale pink to white with a sweet honey-like fragrance that's strongest in the evening

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Opposite pairs of deeply divided, feathery leaves with 7-21 narrow leaflets that feel soft and slightly fuzzy to the touch

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Tall, upright stems growing 3-5 feet high from a spreading underground root system, often forming colonies

idTips.label: Roots
idTips.description: Thick, fibrous roots with a very strong, musky, almost cheese-like smell when crushed or broken - unmistakable once experienced

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small, papery seeds with feathery white plumes that help them float on the wind, appearing after flowers fade

habitat: Common valerian thrives in moist, rich soils along stream banks, wet meadows, and woodland edges throughout New England. You'll often find it in partially shaded areas where the soil stays consistently moist, such as ditches, swales, and the edges of ponds or marshes. It's equally at home in disturbed areas like old farmsteads and can sometimes escape from herb gardens to naturalize nearby.

seasonality.spring: New shoots emerge early with fresh, bright green feathery foliage unfurling from the base. Young leaves are the most tender and easiest to identify by their distinctive deeply-divided shape.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming time from June through August, when the sweet-scented flower clusters are most prominent and fragrant. This is the best season for positive identification using the characteristic flowers.
seasonality.fall: Flowers give way to fluffy seed heads that catch the light beautifully, while leaves begin to yellow and die back. Seeds disperse on autumn winds.
seasonality.winter: Dies back completely to underground roots, leaving no above-ground trace. The persistent root system remains dormant until spring, still retaining its distinctive musky odor if disturbed.

funFact: Valerian root contains compounds that act as a powerful stimulant for cats - even more so than catnip! Wild and domestic cats will dig up the roots, roll in them ecstatically, and become quite 'drunk' on the scent, which explains why valerian was once called 'cat's heal-all.'
confusionNotes: The feathery, divided leaves might be confused with other plants in the carrot family, but valerian's opposite leaf arrangement (leaves growing in pairs across from each other) versus the alternate leaves of most carrot family plants is the key difference. Remember: 'Valerian's leaves pair up, carrot family leaves don't.'
contextualKnowledge: This European native has been so widely cultivated for medicinal use that it's thoroughly naturalized across New England and is often considered a wildflower rather than an introduced species. Many people know it from health food stores as a sleep aid, but may not recognize the living plant in the wild.
compareHints: Common valerian is much taller and more robust than its relative marsh valerian, which stays under 2 feet tall and prefers wetter, more acidic soils. Common valerian's flower clusters are also much more dense and rounded compared to marsh valerian's more open, sparse flower arrangement. The leaf divisions are more numerous and finer in common valerian, giving it a more feathery appearance overall.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Marsh valerian differs from common valerian by being much smaller (1-3 feet vs 3-6 feet), preferring wetlands over disturbed uplands, and having more delicate, feathery foliage.
